definition: Dandelon.com is a search engine for the academic community, started in 2004.
details: The solution was invented in 2001 by Manfred Hauer of AGI and Karl Raedler from Vorarlberger Landesbibliothek, Austria. dandelon.com community is a European pioneer in catalog enrichment. Linked libraries digitize tables of contents of books and capture details of periodicals by using OCR, text analytics, machine translation and put results to catalogues, discovery engines and library sharing centers for cross language and multilingual retrieval.

explainer.lead: Dandelon.com is an academic search engine built around richer library records. By making book tables of contents and periodical details searchable across languages, it helps researchers find material that a title and author search alone might miss.

tiers.eli5: Imagine looking for a book by reading only its title; you might miss one with the perfect chapter inside. Dandelon.com helps libraries turn contents pages and magazine details into searchable information, a bit like adding every chapter title to the library's index. It can also help people search across different languages.
tiers.practitioner: Linked libraries digitize book tables of contents and capture periodical details, then process them with OCR, text analytics, and machine translation. The results feed catalogues, discovery engines, and library sharing centers for cross-language and multilingual retrieval. OCR mistakes and translation quality are practical concerns because they affect the searchable text.
tiers.paperLevel: Dandelon.com can be described as an academic retrieval service over catalog records enriched with digitized book tables of contents and periodical details. Its processing pipeline combines OCR, text analytics, and machine translation to support cross-language and multilingual retrieval. The approach was invented in 2001 by Manfred Hauer of AGI and Karl Raedler of Vorarlberger Landesbibliothek, and the search engine started in 2004.

explainer.example: A student searching in English for a chapter on renewable energy could discover a relevant book whose original contents page is in another language, because the digitized contents have been processed for cross-language retrieval.

explainer.intuition: A book's title rarely tells you everything inside it. Adding its contents page to the searchable record creates many more useful ways to discover it.
howItWorks: Linked libraries digitize book tables of contents.
They also capture details of periodicals.
OCR and text analytics turn the material into usable text and data.
Machine translation supports cross-language and multilingual searching.
The results are supplied to catalogues, discovery engines, and library sharing centers.
explainer.whyItMatters: It makes the inside of books more discoverable and helps library users find relevant material across language boundaries. This is especially useful when a title alone gives little clue that a particular chapter is relevant.
misconceptions: It is not just a search box; linked libraries and catalog enrichment are central to the service.
It does not rely only on book titles and authors; tables of contents and periodical details add searchable depth.
Multilingual retrieval involves processing and translation, not simply storing the original scanned pages.
